title: The series
body:
I trained as a doctor (MBBS) and now work in US healthcare operations: coding, billing audit, risk adjustment, care coordination. Every day I see problems that a small, well-built tool could fix.

So over the past few weeks I've been building them, using AI coding tools (Claude Code) to go from idea to a live demo in days instead of months.

Eight projects so far, all on public or synthetic data:
• DecodeMyBill: explains a medical bill and flags duplicate charges
• Denial Co-pilot: turns a claim denial code into a fix or an appeal
• CivicFeed: what 722 public comments said about a CMS rule
• Discharge Gap Checker: what a nursing home needs but didn't get
• Medicaid Renewal Buddy: New York's 2027 work requirements, in plain language
• Sprain or Fracture?: the Ottawa Rules as a self-check
• Integrative Case Sheet and SIH 2026 Explorer

Over the next two weeks I'll share one at a time: the problem, what I built, and what I learned.

All of them are here: https://rutulpatel.dev

#HealthInformatics #HealthTech #DigitalHealth #BuildInPublic

title: DecodeMyBill
body:
A fake ER bill: $3,974. What Medicare would pay for the same services: $359.

And three errors hidden in it: a metabolic panel billed twice (the basic one is part of the comprehensive one), a blood draw billed three times, and a duplicate chest X-ray. About $668 the patient shouldn't owe.

Most people can't spot that, because bills are written in CPT codes. Only a tiny share of patients ever appeal, yet many of those who do, win.

So I built DecodeMyBill. Paste a bill or snap a photo, and it:
• explains every line in plain English
• compares each charge with Medicare's 2026 rate (computed from the official CMS fee schedules)
• flags duplicates and double billing
• writes a dispute letter and a phone script

Two things I cared about: all price maths happens in code, never in an AI model, and the bill never leaves your browser.

Try it with a fake bill: https://decodemybill.vercel.app
Code: https://github.com/patelr31/decodemybill

#MedicalBilling #HealthcareCosts #PatientAdvocacy #HealthTech

title: Denial Co-pilot
body:
"CO-50 N115." To most people that's noise. To a billing team it means: the payer says the service wasn't medically necessary, based on a Medicare Local Coverage Determination, and the provider is on the hook.

Every denial on a remittance arrives as codes like that. Knowing what to do next, whether to fix and resubmit, appeal, bill another payer or write it off, usually takes someone who has seen hundreds of them.

Denial Co-pilot puts that knowledge in one screen. Enter the codes and get:
• a plain-English explanation
• who is liable (the group code decides it)
• the recommended path and a fix checklist
• Medicare's 120-day appeal deadline, worked out from the denial date
• a draft appeal letter or corrected-claim checklist

Testing on ten made-up denials caught two mistakes in my own first draft. A CO-group "non-covered" denial can never be billed to the patient, and a signed ABN changes CO-50 into PR-50. Both are now built into the rules.

https://denial-copilot.vercel.app

#RevenueCycle #MedicalBilling #ClaimDenials #HealthTech

title: CivicFeed
body:
722 people and organizations commented on CMS's proposed rule on interoperability and prior authorization for drugs. I wanted to know what they actually said.

What I found:
• 36% of the comments came from two coordinated campaigns: a form letter sent 236 times, and a template filed by 16 community health centers, each with its own name swapped in. Simple text matching missed that one; I spotted it while reading the themes.
• Almost nobody opposed the rule. The clearest "withdraw the proposal" comment was about a different rule entirely, probably misfiled.
• The real debate was timing: about 10 times more comments asked CMS to delay or phase in the October 2027 deadline than to hold it.

How it works: code does what rules can (campaign detection, who's commenting, clustering into themes). AI labels and summarises the themes, but writes no numbers. Then code checks that every quote appears word for word in the original comment, or the build fails.

That last step is the one I'd keep on every AI project.

https://civicfeed-six.vercel.app

#HealthPolicy #CMS #Interoperability #PriorAuthorization #AI

title: Discharge Gap Checker
body:
A patient arrives at a nursing home on a Friday evening. The discharge summary lists oxycodone, but there's no signed controlled-substance prescription. The facility pharmacy can't dispense it, and the patient misses their pain doses that night.

Gaps like this are routine. In a national survey of nursing home Directors of Nursing (JAMA Network Open, 2021), behavioral status was missing for 68% of hospital–nursing home pairs, social status for 66%, and an after-hours hospital contact for 54%. Facilities spent about 6.5 hours a week chasing information.

The Discharge Gap Checker reads a pasted discharge summary and shows:
• which of those commonly missing items are absent
• safety flags: an opioid with no prescription, an antibiotic with no stop date, a pending result with no one named to follow it up
• a ready list of callback questions, safety first

I tested it on five synthetic summaries with gaps planted on purpose. It catches all of them.

If you work in post-acute admissions, I'd love to hear what else you'd check.

https://discharge-gap.vercel.app

#CareTransitions #SkilledNursing #PostAcuteCare #PatientSafety

title: Medicaid Renewal Buddy
body:
From January 2027, many New York Medicaid members aged 19–64 face two changes: a work requirement (80 hours a month, or $580 in income) and renewals every 6 months instead of once a year. The state says nearly 2 million New Yorkers are in the affected group.

I used to be a care coordinator, and I know how these changes land: a notice in confusing language, a missed deadline, coverage gone.

So I built a plain-language helper. Answer a few questions to see:
• whether the requirement applies to you, and whether you qualify for an exception (including the planned Bronx exception)
• how your income and hours add up, using the state's own conversion ($380 = 52 hours)
• what to have ready, and when you renew, with calendar reminders

One piece of good news it includes: New York is using a hold-harmless period, so nobody loses coverage over the work requirement before June 30, 2027.

Every rule links to its official source. It's educational, not legal advice.

https://medicaid-buddy.vercel.app

#Medicaid #NewYork #HealthEquity #HealthPolicy

title: Sprain or Fracture?
body:
You twist your ankle. Is it a sprain or a fracture? Usually the only way to find out is an ER visit and an X-ray, and most turn out to be sprains.

Emergency doctors already have a tool for this: the Ottawa Rules. A handful of questions (where it hurts, whether certain bony points are tender, whether you could take 4 steps) decide who needs an X-ray. In pooled studies they catch about 98% of fractures.

I turned them into a guided self-check, for Razorpay's Fix My Itch problem: "Why is distinguishing sprains from fractures impossible without costly hospital visits?"

As a doctor, the order mattered most to me:
1. Warning signs first (deformity, a numb or cold foot, a high-energy injury): go to the ER, no questions asked
2. When the rules don't apply (children, old injuries, head injuries): see a clinician
3. Only then, the Ottawa questions, with a diagram of where to press

It's honest that these rules were built for a clinician's exam, so a self-check is less certain. If in doubt, get checked.

https://patelr31.github.io/sprain-check/

#EmergencyMedicine #EvidenceBasedMedicine #DigitalHealth #FixMyItch

title: Integrative Case Sheet and SIH 2026 Explorer
body:
Two connected builds, because one led to the other.

First I made a dashboard of all 226 Smart India Hackathon 2026 problem statements. Two findings: AI shows up in 44% of the real problems, and the theme labels can't be trusted. A clinical-trials dashboard was filed under Space Technology, and land-record digitisation under MedTech.

Filtering by health instead of by theme surfaced SIH26047, "Patient Case-Taking Software" from the Ministry of Ayush. So I built it:
• a guided case sheet for clinicians who practise Ayush and modern medicine together: history, vitals, a Prakriti screen and the eight-fold Ashtavidha examination
• diagnoses coded in ICD-10-CM from a verified list (checking caught one code that wasn't billable)
• red-flag checks that prompt modern referral, like chest pain on exertion
• export as a FHIR R4 bundle with LOINC-coded vitals, so the record can travel

https://integrative-case-sheet.vercel.app
https://sih-2026-explorer-tau.vercel.app

#FHIR #Interoperability #Ayush #DigitalHealth #SmartIndiaHackathon
